passages.text: But let every door be opened to him, and let all the wretched, enacted laws be dissolved, laws laid down for jealous people. Dominated by folly and unwilling to understand what is reasonable, and also looking suspiciously at the so-called adulterers, these people are reasonably made sport of by Zeus himself through Minos and Rhadamanthys, by means of enacted laws. For Love cannot be restrained once he has taken up residence in souls. The passion of lovers is not voluntary. Indeed, Zeus himself, the lawgiver of these people, had relations with countless women. Some wise men praise him as a benefactor in childbearing, granting human beings union with himself. But among those whom he knew did not recognize the favor, he changed his appearance, so that he would neither distress them nor seem to act against the laws he himself had established. Therefore, for the sake of a good life, you must devote yourself to philosophy and imitate those acknowledged to be superior, whose unions have been countless.

lexical_decisions.chosen: enacted
lexical_decisions.rationale: The laws are instituted or laid down, contrasting humanly established prohibition with the speaker's account of irresistible love. Arbitrary is a possible evaluative reading, but enacted does not add that judgment to the adjective itself.

lexical_decisions.chosen: are reasonably made sport of ... by means of enacted laws
lexical_decisions.rationale: The passive verb describes the jealous people as being played with or mocked, not as themselves playing. The positive judgment reasonably is the letter writer's, and is not silently reversed to match the surrounding narrative's moral position.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: παρ’ οἷς δὲ ἐπὶ τῷ χάριτι ἠπίστατο ἀγνοούμενος
lexical_decisions.chosen: among those whom he knew did not recognize the favor
lexical_decisions.rationale: The masculine passive participle refers to Zeus as unrecognized in respect of the favor. More literally, among those by whom he knew he was unrecognized for the favor. The rendering does not supply a specific husband or woman where the plural leaves the recipients general.

lexical_decisions.chosen: you must devote yourself to philosophy
lexical_decisions.rationale: The feminine participle addresses the female recipient. The main English does not need a gendered pronoun, but retains the instruction to attend to philosophy rather than treating philosophy as an external agent.

passages.text: And so as not to waste time needlessly on further proofs, I will begin with Zeus himself, the father of gods and humans, and disclose some of his unions; recalling them all is impossible because of their number. Listen, then, to the unions of great Zeus himself that were concealed through changes of form because of foolish men's jealousy. First, wishing to remove for the wise the supposed sin of adultery arising from different unions, when he was about to marry, and knowing that, as at a first bed, he was not becoming an adulterer according to most people, he obtained a sinless marriage through the supposed sin, as I said. For he marries Hera, his own sister, having made himself resemble the plumage of a cuckoo. From her Hebe and Eileithyia were born. For he gives birth to Metis without union with anyone, just as Hera gives birth to Hephaestus.

lexical_decisions.chosen: different unions
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adjective can indicate differing or varied unions. The context presents the writer's attempt to remove the charge of adultery from multiple unions, but the phrase is not expanded to specify particular partners not named here.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ ὡς ἐπὶ πρώτῃ εὐνῇ κατὰ τοὺς πολλοὺς μοιχὸς εἰδὼς οὐ γινόμενος
lexical_decisions.chosen: and knowing that, as at a first bed, he was not becoming an adulterer according to most people
lexical_decisions.rationale: The unusual first-bed comparison and the appeal to most people's judgment are both preserved. Bed is a sexual or marital union here. The nominative participles are read as Zeus's knowledge of his own not becoming an adulterer; an alternative takes knowing and not becoming as parallel descriptions. The main text does not resolve the argument into an unstated rule about either partner's previous marital status.

lexical_decisions.chosen: having made himself resemble the plumage of a cuckoo
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative literally names a cuckoo's feather or plumage. Plumage preserves that expressed image rather than simply replacing it with the whole bird; a cuckoo's feather is a narrower alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν Μῆτιν γὰρ χωρὶς τῆς πρὸς τινὰ μίξεως ἀποκυΐσκει
lexical_decisions.chosen: For he gives birth to Metis without union with anyone
lexical_decisions.rationale: The active verb assigns the birth to Zeus. The supplied name and unusual parentage are retained rather than harmonized with other versions of the myth.

passages.text: He also has relations with a sister born to him from Uranus and Sea through Cronus's castration, .... Eros and Cypris, whom they also call Didone. He also has relations with Antiope, daughter of Nycteus, having made himself like a satyr; from her Amphion and Zethus were born. He unites with Alcmene, Amphitryon's wife, resembling Amphitryon her husband; from her Heracles was born. He also approaches Aegina, daughter of Asopus, becoming an eagle; from her Aeacus is born. He lies with Amalthea, daughter of Phocus, resembling a bear. He flowed down upon Danae, daughter of Acrisius, as gold; from her Perseus flew forth. For Callisto, daughter of Lycaon, he became a fierce lion, and she bears another, Arcas. He united with Europa, daughter of Phoenix, through a bull; from her Minos, Rhadamanthys, and Sarpedon sprang forth. With Eurymedusa, daughter of Achelous, he became an ant; from her came Myrmidon. With the nymph of Hersaeus he became a vulture; from her came the Palici in Sicily. He united with earth-born Himalia in Rhodes through rain; from her came Spartaeus, Cronius, and Cytus. He took Cassiopeia as a bride, resembling Phoenix her husband; from her Atymnius sprang forth for him. With Nemesis, daughter of Thestius, who was also considered Leda, he became a swan or a goose and fathered Helen; and again, becoming a star, he brought forth Castor and Polydeuces. For Lamia he changed into a hoopoe.

lexical_decisions.chosen: through Cronus's castration
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive can describe a castration associated with Cronus as agent or as the person castrated. Castration carried out by Cronus is a material alternative. The possessive English preserves the association without supplying an otherwise unnamed victim in this clause.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ἔρως καὶ Κύπρις, ἣν καὶ Διδώνην λέγουσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Eros and Cypris, whom they also call Didone
lexical_decisions.rationale: The two names after the printed gap remain a fragment, without an invented verb or genealogical connection. The feminine relative refers to Cypris. Didone transliterates the printed name rather than silently correcting it to Dione.

lexical_decisions.chosen: from her Perseus flew forth
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb's flight image is retained. Sprang forth would be a more idiomatic birth expression but would conceal the explicit flying verb.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Καλλιστοῖ τῇ Λυκάονος ἠγριώθη λέων, καὶ ἄλλον τίκτει Ἀρκάδα
lexical_decisions.chosen: For Callisto, daughter of Lycaon, he became a fierce lion, and she bears another, Arcas
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied lion form and the word another are retained without harmonizing other accounts. The subject of bears is inferred as Callisto from the reproductive context; the masculine Arcas identifies the child.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the nymph of Hersaeus
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive relationship is left broad. Νύμφη can also mean bride or young wife, so bride of Hersaeus is a material alternative. The text is not expanded into a specific genealogy or a different familiar myth.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Νεμέσει τῇ Θεστίου, τῇ καὶ Λήδᾳ νομισθείσῃ, κύκνος ἢ χὴν γενόμενος
lexical_decisions.chosen: With Nemesis, daughter of Thestius, who was also considered Leda, he became a swan or a goose
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both the alternative bird forms and the source's identification of Nemesis with Leda are preserved rather than choosing a single familiar version.

source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints a four-dot gap. The English retains exactly four dots and the following fragment Eros and Cypris, without inventing the lost connection or restoring a missing birth statement. The surviving passage is not represented as an unbroken original.

passages.text: Resembling a shepherd, he makes Mnemosyne the mother of the Muses. He marries Semele, daughter of Cadmus, while blazing, and from her brings forth Dionysus. He himself takes his daughter Persephone as a bride, having made himself like a serpent; she was also considered the wife of his brother Pluto. He has relations with many other women even without changing form, their husbands feeling no jealousy as though over a sin, but knowing well that by freely sharing in union with their wives he fathers children, granting them Hermeses, Apollos, Dionysuses, Endymions, and all the others we have mentioned, outstanding in beauty from union with him.

lexical_decisions.chosen: while blazing
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle describes Zeus as flaming or blazing. The translation does not supply a specific material body or explain the event using a different familiar account.

lexical_decisions.chosen: He himself takes his daughter Persephone as a bride
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb can concern marrying off or taking in marriage. The reflexive emphasis and the sexual sequence favor Zeus himself as the participant taking his daughter as a bride; the alternative of his giving her in marriage remains lexically possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Hermeses, Apollos, Dionysuses, Endymions
lexical_decisions.rationale: The source prints these names in the plural. The English preserves that conspicuous pattern rather than normalizing them to singular named children; it can characterize children of the named divine types.

lexical_decisions.chosen: freely
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adverb may express abundance or the absence of jealousy or grudging. Freely keeps both generosity and lack of restraint available without adding the claim that every husband consented.

passages.text: So that I do not spend my time on an endless account, you will find ungrudging unions among all the gods along with Zeus—unions that foolish people call adulteries of the gods. They do not even avoid unions with males as shameful, but practice this too as something becoming. Thus Zeus himself loves Ganymede; Poseidon, Pelops; Apollo, Cinyras, Zacynthus, Hyacinthus, Phorbas, Hylas, Admetus, Cyparissus, Amyclas, Troilus, Branchus, Atymnius, Parus, Potnieus, and Orpheus; Dionysus, Adonis, Ampelus, Hymenaeus, Hermaphroditus, and Achilles; Asclepius, Hippolytus; Hephaestus, Peleus; Pan, Daphnis; Hermes, Perseus, Chrysus, Thersus, and Odrysus; and Heracles, Abderus, Dryops, Iocastus, Philoctetes, Ilas, Polyphemus, Haemon, Diomus, and Pirithous.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πάντων μετὰ Διὸς θεῶν ἀφθόνους εὑρήσεις κοινωνίας
lexical_decisions.chosen: ungrudging unions
lexical_decisions.rationale: The source separates this adjective and noun with the verb. The adjective can mean abundant or free from jealousy and grudging; the argument against jealousy supports ungrudging, while abundant unions is a material alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Zeus himself loves Ganymede
lexical_decisions.rationale: The stated erotic love supplies the understood verb for the ensuing series of gods and their named male beloveds. The English preserves every listed person and does not add ages or acts beyond the source.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Hylas
lexical_decisions.rationale: This name in Apollo's list begins with upsilon and a rough breathing. It is distinguished in transliteration from the printed Ἴλα in Heracles' list rather than silently treating the two spellings as identical.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Ilas
lexical_decisions.rationale: The printed iota spelling in Heracles' list is retained as Ilas. Identification with the Hylas in Apollo's list is possible but is not imposed on the source text.

passages.text: I have therefore set before you some of the loves of all the more prominent gods, dearest, so that you may know that only foolish human beings experience jealousy over this. That is also why they are mortal and pass their lives in sorrow: because, through their own jealousy, they have declared evil the things that seemed good to the gods. From now on, then, you will be blessed if you imitate gods rather than humans. For when people see you preserving what is considered chastity, they praise you because of their own passion, but do not benefit you. But when the gods see you becoming like themselves, they will both praise and benefit you.

lexical_decisions.chosen: some of the loves
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase signals partial coverage of each set of loves, not an exhaustive account. Loves can also be rendered love affairs in this context.

lexical_decisions.chosen: what is considered chastity
lexical_decisions.rationale: The qualifier marks the letter writer's skeptical treatment of conventional sexual restraint. It is not removed to make the writer endorse chastity, nor does the English adopt his skepticism as the translator's own judgment.

lexical_decisions.chosen: because of their own passion
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun can indicate emotion or a condition of suffering; the surrounding jealousy makes a possessive passion the likely reference. The main text leaves its precise emotional identity implicit rather than inserting a new named motive.

passages.text: Consider for me how many beloved women they rewarded: some they made into constellations, and for some they benefited both children and helpers. Thus Zeus made Callisto into a constellation, the one called the Little Bear, which some also call the Dog's Tail. Poseidon placed Dolphin in heaven because of Amphitrite, and counted Orion, born of Euryale daughter of Minos, worthy of the stars because of Euryale his mother. Dionysus did so with Ariadne's crown. Zeus assigned the eagle that helped in the abduction of Ganymede, and Ganymede himself, a place with the honor of Aquarius; and he honored the bull because of Europa. Moreover, as a favor to Leda, he made Castor, Polydeuces, and Helen into stars; Perseus because of Danae; Arcas because of Callisto; the Maiden, also called Justice, because of Themis; and Heracles because of Alcmene. I will not go on any longer. It would take a long time to detail how many others the gods have benefited because of their many beloved women, through their unions with humans. Foolish people forbid these unions as evil acts, not knowing that pleasure is the great enjoyment among humans.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν λεγομένην ἄρκτον μικράν, ἣν καὶ κυνὸς οὐρὰν προσαγορεύουσίν τινες
lexical_decisions.chosen: the one called the Little Bear, which some also call the Dog's Tail
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both constellation designations and their attribution to Callisto are retained exactly, without harmonizing the passage with a different astronomical identification.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Dionysus did so with Ariadne's crown
lexical_decisions.rationale: The source is an elliptical clause, carrying over the preceding placement among the stars. Did so supplies only that established predicate, not a new celestial act.

lexical_decisions.chosen: assigned ... a place with the honor of Aquarius
lexical_decisions.rationale: Aquarius translates the constellation title Water-Pourer by its conventional English name. The wording attaches the honor to Zeus's assignment; the extent to which the eagle shares the Aquarius description is not resolved by adding a different constellation for it.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the Maiden, also called Justice
lexical_decisions.rationale: The feminine designation is translated as the Maiden, with Justice retaining the meaning of Dike. The source's stray full stop is not treated as a lost-word marker or expanded into an extra gap.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡδονή ἐστιν ἡ μεγάλη ἐν ἀνθρώποις ἀπόλαυσις
lexical_decisions.chosen: pleasure is the great enjoyment among humans
lexical_decisions.rationale: The near repetition of pleasure and enjoyment belongs to the source's maxim. It is retained rather than replaced by a stronger claim that pleasure is the only good or purpose of human life.

passages.text: What then? Do not even the celebrated wise men prefer pleasure and have relations with whichever women they wished? First among them is the teacher of Greece, about whom Phoebus himself said, ‘Of all men, Socrates is wisest.’ Does he not propose that women be held in common in the best-governed city, Lacedaemon, and cover the handsome Alcibiades beneath his cloak? The Socratic Antisthenes also writes that one should not reject so-called adultery. And does not his pupil Diogenes openly have relations with Lais, in return for carrying her publicly on his shoulders? Does not Epicurus prefer pleasure? Does not Aristippus, perfumed all over, give himself to Aphrodite? Does not Zeno, hinting at treating things as indifferent, say that the divine is present through everything, so that intelligent people may recognize that, with whomever someone has relations, he has relations as with himself, and that forbidding so-called adulteries or unions with a mother, daughter, sister, or children is superfluous? Chrysippus, in his love letters, also mentions the image in Argos, placing Hera's face at Zeus's genitals.

lexical_decisions.chosen: propose that women be held in common
lexical_decisions.rationale: The claim is assigned to Socrates in the source and retained as the letter writer's claim. It is not silently reassigned to another philosopher or rewritten into a historically corrected account.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπὶ μισθῷ τοῦ φέρειν αὐτὴν ἐπ’ ὤμων δημοσίᾳ
lexical_decisions.chosen: in return for carrying her publicly on his shoulders
lexical_decisions.rationale: The infinitive specifies the payment or recompense as carrying Lais. The rendering does not add money, identify a fee amount, or reverse who carries whom.

lexical_decisions.chosen: hinting at treating things as indifferent
lexical_decisions.rationale: Indifference is the philosophical treatment of the acts as morally neither good nor bad, not simply emotional unconcern. The source presents this as an indirect implication, retained as hinting rather than an explicit quotation from Zeno.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μίξεις μητρὸς ἢ θυγατρὸς ἢ ἀδελφῆς ἢ παίδων
lexical_decisions.chosen: unions with a mother, daughter, sister, or children
lexical_decisions.rationale: Children preserves the broad age and relationship range of παῖδες. Boys is possible in this sexual context, but the adjacent family categories also support children; the source does not name particular ages.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρὸς τῷ τοῦ Διὸς αἰδοίῳ φέρων τῆς Ἥρας τὸ πρόσωπον
lexical_decisions.chosen: placing Hera's face at Zeus's genitals
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle concerns the writer's description of the image. The precise position is retained without adding an act not expressly named in the supplied wording.

passages.text: I know that these things appear terrifying and utterly shameful to those uninitiated in the truth, but not to the gods and philosophers of the Greeks, nor to the mysteries of Dionysus and Demeter. But, after all this, so that I do not waste time recounting the lives of every god and philosopher, let two be your greatest models: Zeus among gods, and Socrates among human philosophers. For the rest, understand what I have reminded you of in writing, and take care never to distress a lover of yours. For if you act against gods and lovers, you will be judged impious and undergo the appropriate punishment. But if you offer yourself to every lover, then, as an imitator of the gods, you will obtain their beneficence. For the rest, dearest, remember the mysteries I have disclosed to you and show me your decision in writing. Farewell.

lexical_decisions.chosen: those uninitiated in the truth
lexical_decisions.rationale: The initiation image is explicit and continues into the reference to mysteries. Uninformed would be smoother but would erase the writer's claim to privileged initiatory knowledge.

lexical_decisions.chosen: let two be your greatest models
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun can mean marks, aims, or objects of attention. The two exemplary figures and the subsequent imitation argument favor models; the rendering does not make them legal authorities or assign a new office.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐὰν δὲ παντὶ ἐραστῇ ἑαυτὴν παράσχῃς
lexical_decisions.chosen: if you offer yourself to every lover
lexical_decisions.rationale: The universal every and reflexive yourself are retained as the letter writer's demand. The translation reports his coercive argument without adopting it or adding detail.

passages.text: So I took this document from Apion as though I really intended to send it to the beloved woman. I fabricated a reply as though she had written back to these things, and when Apion came the next day, I gave it to him as her supposed reply. It read as follows:

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπλασάμην ὡς ἐκείνης πρὸς ταῦτα ἀντιγραψάσης
lexical_decisions.chosen: I fabricated a reply as though she had written back to these things
lexical_decisions.rationale: The narrator explicitly claims authorship of the fictional response. It is not presented as an authentic letter from the woman or as a mere transcription of one.

lexical_decisions.chosen: this document
lexical_decisions.rationale: The object is the preceding written letter, not necessarily a codex or full-length book. Document preserves the written artifact without imposing a modern book format.

passages.text: Copy of a letter to Apion, supposedly from the beloved woman. I am amazed that, after praising me for wisdom, you write to me as though I were foolish. For, wishing to persuade me into your passion, you made your examples from the myths about the gods, not afraid to blaspheme Love, the oldest of all, as you said, upon that of all gods and humans, so that you might corrupt my soul and outrage my body. For love that consists in desires is not the leader of the gods. If he desires willingly, he is his own passion and punishment, and one who willingly suffers would not be a god. But if he unwillingly loves sexual union and, passing through our souls, is carried through our bodies as through instruments into unions with intelligible beings, then whoever makes him love and carries him is greater than he is. And again, if that very one who carries him is carried by another longing, another, greater one is found who carries that one, and an endless regress of lovers results, which is impossible. Thus there is neither one who carries nor one who is carried; rather, it is the lover's own desiring passion, increased by hope and diminished by despair.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ἀντίγραφον ἐπιστολῆς πρὸς Ἀππίωνα ὡς παρὰ τῆς ἐρωμένης
lexical_decisions.chosen: Copy of a letter to Apion, supposedly from the beloved woman
lexical_decisions.rationale: The heading and its qualification are translated as supplied. The preceding section makes the supposed female authorship part of the narrator's fabrication.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἔρως γὰρ θεῶν οὐκ ἔστιν ἀρχηγέτης ὁ ἐν ταῖς ἐπιθυμίαις
lexical_decisions.chosen: For love that consists in desires is not the leader of the gods
lexical_decisions.rationale: The restriction identifies the love manifested in desires. Leader can also be originator or founding source; the argument denies that this passion rules or originates the gods, without settling a separate metaphysical theory of all forms of love.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς τὰς τῶν νοητῶν φέρεται συνουσίας
lexical_decisions.chosen: is carried ... into unions with intelligible beings
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied νοητῶν concerns what is apprehensible to thought, not a silently corrected reference to mortal beings. With intelligible beings takes the genitive as the partners of union; unions of intelligible beings is a material alternative that leaves their relation broader. The unusual metaphysical reference is retained without inventing physical partners.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς ἀπέραντον ἐπαναφορὰ τῶν ἐρώντων γίνεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: an endless regress of lovers results
lexical_decisions.rationale: The repeated appeal to a greater mover generates an unending backward sequence. Regress renders that argumentative sequence rather than suggesting a recurring cycle at one level.

source_issues.source_quote: ἐπὶ τῆς πάντων θεῶν καὶ ἀνθρώπων
source_issues.issue: The supplied phrase has the feminine genitive article τῆς without an identifiable expressed feminine head. The English's equally unresolved ‘upon that of all gods and humans’ is only a literal placeholder, not a claim to recover its meaning. The construction needs source-level or scholarly resolution before publication; no missing noun, clause, or printed dot gap has been invented.

passages.text: Those unwilling to master shameful desire tell lies about the gods, so that, by pointing to the gods as having done first the things they themselves do, they may escape blame. For if the so-called gods committed adulteries for the sake of having children and not sexual excess, why did they also have relations with males? ‘But,’ he says, ‘as a favor to their beloved women, they made them into constellations.’ So were there no stars before this, until heaven was adorned with stars by adulterers on the pretext of sexual excess? And how is it that the descendants of those made into constellations are punished in Hades: Atlas weighed down, Tantalus tormented by thirst, Sisyphus pushing a rock, Tityus having his entrails dug into, and Ixion rolling endlessly around a wheel? And how is it that the lovers, being gods, made those whom they defiled into constellations, without granting this favor to themselves?

lexical_decisions.chosen: sexual excess
lexical_decisions.rationale: The term describes unrestrained or shameless sexual conduct in this argument. The same rendering is maintained in the two occurrences rather than replacing the second by an invented account of how constellations were formed.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the descendants of those made into constellations
lexical_decisions.rationale: The relationship and direction of descent are retained as the speaker's claim. They are not changed to ancestors or to the constellated figures themselves to harmonize the list with other myths.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Tityus having his entrails dug into
lexical_decisions.rationale: The passive suffering and the body part are retained. No animal, instrument, or additional violent detail absent from this clause is supplied.

passages.text: They were not gods, then, but veiled representations of tyrants. For a tomb of Cronus is shown in the Caucasian mountains—not in heaven but on earth—the tomb of a savage man who devoured his children. A tomb of the sexually unrestrained Zeus of myth, who likewise swallowed his daughter Metis, is also seen in Crete. There is also Pluto's tomb at the Acherusian lake, Poseidon's on Tenos, the Sun's at Atroi and the Moon's at Carrhae, Hermes' at Hermopolis, Ares' in Thrace, Aphrodite's on Cyprus, Dionysus' at Thebes, and those of others in other places. In any case, the tombs of the very gods mentioned are visible. For they were humans, and wicked ones and sorcerers at that. They could not otherwise have become absolute rulers—I mean the Zeus of myth and Dionysus—unless through transformation they gained control over whomever they wished for whatever purpose they themselves wished.

lexical_decisions.chosen: veiled representations of tyrants
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun denotes enigmatic or figurative representations. The claim identifies the mythic gods as disguised presentations of human tyrants, not merely difficult riddles that tyrants posed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ἡλίου δὲ ἐν Ἄτροις καὶ Σελήνης ἐν Κάρραις
lexical_decisions.chosen: the Sun's at Atroi and the Moon's at Carrhae
lexical_decisions.rationale: The divine names are rendered by their transparent celestial meanings; Helios and Selene are conventional name alternatives. Atroi follows the supplied place-name spelling without silently identifying it with another city.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰ μὴ τῇ μεταμορφώσει ὧν ἤθελον ἐπεκράτουν εἰς ὅπερ αὐτοὶ ἤθελον
lexical_decisions.chosen: unless through transformation they gained control over whomever they wished for whatever purpose they themselves wished
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive after gained control is read as those controlled, and the final phrase as the intended end. The wording does not specify whether the transformation is their own or that of others, nor explain an otherwise unnamed magical mechanism.

passages.text: If we must emulate their lives, let us imitate not only their adulteries but also their tables. For Cronus swallowed his own children, and Zeus likewise his own daughter. And what need is there to say more? Pelops became a dinner for all the gods. So let us too, before our unlawful marriages, hold a similar dinner to the gods'. Then the dinner would be worthy of the marriages. But you would never bear to do this, just as I would never bear to commit adultery. Besides all this, you threaten me with the wrath of Love as though he were a powerful god. Love is not a god such as he is thought to be, but a desire arising from the constitution of the living being for the succession of life, according to the providence of the one who brought everything into being. This is so that the whole race may never fail, but, on the pretext of pleasure, another may again come into being from the substance of the one who is going to die, sprung from a lawful marriage, so that he may know his own father in order to support him in old age. Those born from adultery would not be able to do this, lacking a natural affection toward those who begot them.

lexical_decisions.chosen: And what need is there to say more?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rhetorical question concerns what needs saying, not what one is able to say. More is supplied from the movement toward the final example, rather than changing the question into an appeal to ability.

lexical_decisions.chosen: from the constitution of the living being
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun refers to the mixture or constitution of the organism. Animal is another literal rendering of ζῷον, but living being preserves its applicability to humans in this explanation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: on the pretext of pleasure
lexical_decisions.rationale: The same pretext language used in the polemic is retained in the positive account of generation. For the sake of pleasure would flatten the distinction between the reproductive purpose and the pleasure that provides its occasion.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὅπως πρὸς τὸ γηροτροφεῖν τὸν αὐτοῦ πατέρα γνώσῃ
lexical_decisions.chosen: so that he may know his own father in order to support him in old age
lexical_decisions.rationale: The child is the inferred subject of knowing, with the father its expressed object and support in old age the purpose. The source's ensuing assertion about children born from adultery is retained as the fictional letter writer's claim, not presented as an established psychological fact.

passages.text: Since, then, erotic desire arises for the sake of succession and legitimate increase, as I said, parents should take thought for chastity and educate their children in advance, before desire arises, through books that teach self-restraint. They should accustom them beforehand to better teachings, because habit is a second nature. In addition, they should frequently remind them of the punishments imposed by the laws, so that, using fear like a bridle, they do not rush along with improper pleasures. It is also fitting to satisfy through marriage the natural passion of their age before desire reaches its height, having first persuaded them not to fix their eyes on the figure of a courtesan.

lexical_decisions.chosen: legitimate increase
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adjective concerns legitimate descent in the contrast with adultery. Genuine growth is a more literal lexical alternative, but would obscure the explicitly marital context.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: σωφροσύνης προνοουμένους, τοὺς αὐτῶν παῖδας πρὸ τῆς ἐπιθυμίας διὰ τῶν σωφρονιζόντων βιβλίων
lexical_decisions.chosen: take thought for chastity ... through books that teach self-restraint
lexical_decisions.rationale: The shared word-family concerns restraint, here especially sexual chastity. The English varies the cognate forms for natural readability while disclosing their connection; books that teach chastity is a narrower alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρὸ τοῦ τὴν ἐπιθυμίαν ἐπακμάσαι γάμῳ τὸ φυσικὸν τῆς ἡλικίας πληροφορεῖν πάθος
lexical_decisions.chosen: satisfy through marriage the natural passion of their age before desire reaches its height
lexical_decisions.rationale: The ancient recommendation and its timing are retained without turning them into present-day guidance or adding an age not stated in the source. The verb denotes filling or satisfying the passion, not merely recognizing it.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς εἶδος ἑταίρας γυναικὸς μὴ ἀτενίζειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: not to fix their eyes on the figure of a courtesan
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied ἑταίρας is read as the noun courtesan, not silently changed to ἑτέρας, another. Figure renders visible form or appearance without adding the adjective beautiful.
